newsitem.title: UK: Britain clamps down on drug company freebies.
newsitem.headline: Britain clamps down on drug company freebies.

text.p: Britain's health ministry said on Monday it would clamp down on drugs companies that tried to bribe doctors and pharmacists into using their products.
Only gifts of nominal value, related to medicine, were allowed, the ministry said in a statement.
"We will not tolerate unlawful promotions which seek to exert improper influence," Health Minister Baroness Jay said.
The Medicines Control Agency said it had sent a letter to pharmaceutical companies and to professional bodies representing doctors and pharmacists, reminding them of the law.
The government said it was worried by reports that companies were offering electrical goods, stereo systems, video cameras and even holidays as inducements to use their products.
Pharmaceutical companies or doctors, dentists, pharmacists or sales staff who break the regulations risk a fine of 5,000 pounds ($8,280) and two years in prison.
Small gifts like pens or notepads are all right, the government says.
"It is a criminal offence for any person to offer gifts, pecuniary advantages or benefits in kind as an inducement to prescribe or supply their medicines," the ministry said.
"Examples of unlawful promotions include 'bonus points' entitling health professionals to gifts like air miles, holiday discounts (and) mountain bikes," Jay added.
Last year Norton Healthcare, Britain's largest distributor of non-branded drugs, was scolded for breaching the Association of British Pharmaceutical Industry's (ABPI) voluntary clode of practice.
The company resigned from the ABPI in protest.
It had run an advertisement in a trade magazine, offering pharmacists vouchers at Marks & Spencer department stores if they spent 600 pounds on Norton's hay fever drug Terfenadine forte.
Those who spent more could get a mountain bike.
ABPI spokesman Richard Ley said the industry acted quickly once it learned of the ads. "When we have information this sort of thing is taking place, then it's investigated," he said.
